short: Cuneus equitum - a spearhead, a wedge of horsemen, it is a wedge-shaped battle formation used to concentrate the onslaught and break through the enemy formation. The term cuneus has been used in Latin literature and historiography since at least the time of Cato the Elder. Originally, this term served to describe a deep and tight battle formation, such as the Macedonian phalanx. In late Roman literary sources, the term cuneus is used as a designation for various cavalry units. It is assumed that the cunei were separated by Constantine I from the equites which were formed under Diocletian on the basis of the old cavalry units. The fact that several units of cuneus have received the status of Comitatenses (according to Notita Dignitatum), can testify about high combat efficiency of these units. Most likely these units were armed with contus (Ancient Greek kontos, «bear spear»; Latin contus) - a huge spear. Flavius Arrian calls such horsemen by their main offensive weapon – «kontos» - kontophori. Apparently, the most common principle of the contus operation was the same as that of the Parthian cataphractarians' lances: since the great length and heaviness of the lance hampered the rider's action, it was fixed on the body of the horse.
history: One of the simplest forms of one-armed catapult, the onager relied on twisted skeins of animal sinew which provided the power to hurl either rocks or shot. Inaccurate but powerful, it was an effective siege machine against buildings and fortifications, but was of far less use on the battlefield unless firing into massed infantry ranks. First mentioned by Philon of Byzantium in his treatise on ‘Mechanics’, the onager made use of a sling-like cradle attached to a firing arm. This arm was inserted, twisted, and propelled rocks or shot through torsion. As the firing arm was released, the sling-like cradle would unhook, firing the projectile. A padded beam was incorporated into the housing frame to restrain the arm. Larger machines could require as many as eight or ten crewmen, and the incredible recoil meant that they could not be easily or safely mounted on walls or towers. Quickly constructed wherever wood was readily available, onagers soon became a staple of ancient siege warfare.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
